catalog_quote: David 2014 p.15: "3.1.3 Stress. Word stress in Pashto is assigned lexically. In our transcription of Pashto, we indicate stressed syllables by putting an acute accent mark over the vowel portion: /saṛáy/ 'man', /žə́ba/ 'tongue'. Some words differ only by the placement of stress, as with the pronouns /haɣə́/ 'he/she/it' vs. /háɣə/ 'that', or continuous versus aorist forms among second and third conjugation verbs (Section 8.2.5.4 and Section 8.2.5.5)." (sec. 4.2:) "The approach we take in this work assumes five dialects: Southwest (SW), Southeast (SE), Northwest (NW), Northeast (NE) and Middle (M)." ... "Kandahar corresponds to our SW dialect". new_statements.quote: Basic word stress. In every word of more than one syllable, one of the syllables bears heavy stress: it is pronounced with more emphasis and probably with slightly higher pitch than syllables with weaker stress. [...] The location of the heavy stress (whether on the last syllable, the next-to-last, or one of the earlier syllables) is not predictable in Pashto, and the spelling system does not mark stress at all. [...] The stress in native Pashto words is generally on the last syllable if the syllable ends in a consonant, and on the next-to-last (penultimate) syllable if the last syllable ends in a vowel [...] There are probably as many exceptions to the rule given above as there are words which follow it, however, including the word for the language: 'Pashto' [paxtó].

new_statements.rule_in_words: Every polysyllabic word has one heavy (primary) stress, but its position (final, penultimate or earlier) is not predictable and is not. As a tendency, native words are stressed on the final syllable when it is closed (ends in a consonant, e.g. randzúr 'sick' m.) and on the penult when the word ends in a vowel (randzúra 'sick' f.); the authors say the exceptions are probably as numerous as the conforming words. Sources of exceptions: loans keep their source-language stress (Persian -á final-stressed: abá, atyá, ashná; Arabic -a words not: áma, búbala), certain affixes are inherently stressed (plural -úna: yarghalúna; verbalizer -éẓ-: rawanéẓam), and there are many stress minimal pairs (tánga 'pear tree' vs tangá 'cart', áspa 'mare' vs aspá 'spotted fever', kenastá 'he's sitting' vs kénasta 'he sat'). At sentence level the negative particle ná and the perfective particle wə́ always take heavy stress, shifting it off the verb (khwrí 'he's eating' vs ná khwri; daredə́m 'I was standing' vs wə́daredəm 'I stood').
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 27 'Secondary stresses': stress patterns in polysyllabic words and phrases 'have not been studied to any great extent'; the authors note there 'seem to be secondary stresses in Pashto as well as primary stresses', e.g. in wə́daredəm 'I stood' the syllable -ed- is heavier than final -əm but lighter than primary-stressed wə́, and the first syllable of akhistúnkay 'buyer' seems heavier than the second or fourth.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 25: 'probably as many exceptions.. as there are words which follow it', including paxtó 'Pashto'; borrowings keep source stress (Persian final -á vs Arabic non-final); stress minimal pairs; p. 26: inherently stressed affixes (-úna, -éẓ-) and sentence particles ná, wə́ that take heavy stress; p. 31 (PDF 44): loanword motár 'car' has shifted stress from first to last syllable to resemble native words.
new_statements.identity_note: Tegey & Robson 1996 describe the central (Kabul) dialect ('we will describe the consonants and vowels of the central dialect', p. 11) and treat the Kandahar/western dialect only in a short dialect-differences section (pp. 28-29) limited to consonant and diphthong correspondences, with no dialect-specific remark on stress; their stress section is framed as general Pashto. The only listed work explicitly about the Kandahar dialect (Penzl 1955) could not be opened. The catalog entry is for the Southwest/Kandahar dialect, so the Tegey statement should be filed as a general-Pashto (central-dialect-based) statement applied to sout2649 with that caveat.

audit.reasoning: (1) Both deciding quotations are present verbatim at the stated places in copies we hold: David 2014 p.15 sec. 3.1.3 (text layer) and the dialect-scope sentences in sec. 4.2/p.43; Tegey & Robson 1996 pp.24-27 in the held scanned of ERIC ED399825 PDF pp.37-40 (scanned noise only). (2) The classification lexical rests on a 2014 De Gruyter reference grammar that explicitly covers SW=Kandahar and states lexical assignment with stress-only minimal pairs, seconded by the 1996 CAL reference grammar; two open sources downloaded now (Trofimov 2023 JLR, summarising Bečka 1969's stress monograph; Rognoni et al. 2017 Interspeech with 5 SW speakers) agree that Pashto stress is free/unpredictable, adding only the refinement that a majority (68.3%) of words are final-stressed and that many suffixes are inherently stressed, which the record's the primary-stress rule/morphology note already captures via T&R. sources.quote: '[10 = Tegey & Robson 1996] reports that word stress is not predictable in Pashto: generally, it is located on the last or on the penultimate syllable of a word, but (as in Persian), the presence of affixes and other particles often reconfigures stress placement.' Instrumental study of intonation (28 speakers, 5 SW) on telephone speech; no independent word-stress analysis and no dialect difference in stress reported.
